# How Bodhidharma got its accent back

The ASCII form *bodhidharma* is missing something. **Bodhidharma** restores the ​marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full scholarly ‌record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Chinese characters evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. By the end, ‌the marks in Bodhidharma will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Bodhidharma
- **ASCII form:** bodhidharma
- ​**Meaning:** "Dharma of awakening"
- **Domain of influence:** Zen Patriarch, Wall-Gazer
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 菩提達磨 (Chinese characters)

## Overview

**Bodhidharma** (*bodhidharma*) — The Dharma of Awakening, First Patriarch · Dharma of ​awakening — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Zen Patriarch, Wall-Gazer". The name means "Dharma of awakening".

**Bodhidharma** is the First Patriarch of Zen: the Indian prince-turned-monk ​who crossed the Pamirs to China around 520 CE, sat facing a wall at Shaolin for nine years, and transmitted the Buddha’s wordless teaching outside the scriptures. His legend is the bridge between ​India and East Asia — and the seed of martial, meditative, and cultural traditions that span the continent.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Bodhidharma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/bodhidharma/). The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *bodhidharma* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is ‌the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Chinese characters as **菩提達磨**. Etymologically it means "Dharma of awakening".

The ASCII form *bodhidharma* survives only because ​the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Bodhidharma** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the ​address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Chinese characters as **菩提達磨**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *bodhidharma* ‌and the PuniCodex restoration **Bodhidharma** are measured: the restoration preserves its full diacritic detail of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The ​reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˌboʊdɪˈdɑːrmə/** — Sanskrit → Chinese transmission (Pútídámó).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Bodhi-** — From Sanskrit bodhi, “awakening” — the name begins in the Buddha’s own enlightenment-word.
- **-dhar-** — ‌From √dhṛ, “to hold, sustain” — the same root as dharma’s “that which holds”.
- **-ma** — The Chinese rendered it 菩提達磨 (Pútídámó); the Japanese, Daruma; the West, Bodhidharma.

For the modern speaker, the ​closest approximation is: “boh-dee-DAR-muh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — Pútídámó 菩提達磨 — the First Patriarch
- **Japanese** — Daruma 達磨 — the roly-poly doll is his image

The name means ​“awakening-perfection” or “dharma of awakening” — the Indian prince who carried Zen to China.

## Mythology

Bodhidharma’s mythology is a layer-cake of history and legend: the historical missionary of the early sixth century; the ​wall-gazer of the Zen records; the Shaolin temple’s patron of the martial arts; and Japan’s round Daruma doll, whose blank eyes you fill in when your wish comes true. The legend grew because ​the teaching needed a body — and the body it chose was defiant, foreign, and perfectly still.

### The Crossing to China (Transmission Records)

The Zen records send him to the court of the ​Liang emperor Wudi — the great Buddhist patron who asks, ‘what is the highest meaning of the holy truth?’ and is told ‘vast emptiness, nothing holy’. The emperor, scandalized, asks who stands before ‌him: ‘Don’t know’, says the future patriarch, and leaves for the north. The dialogue founded the Zen interview-style in a single exchange.

### Nine Years, One Wall (Wall-Gazing Legend)

At Shaolin he sat facing ​a wall nine years; legend adds that in frustration at sleep he cut off his eyelids — and tea, the meditator’s ally, sprang from where they fell. Huike, his future successor, stood in ‌the snow and cut off his own arm to prove his sincerity; Bodhidharma accepted him and transmitted the teaching. The tradition’s founding images are all of this order: resolve measured in what one ​will lose.

### The Temple and the Arts (Shaolin Cycle)

The legend that he taught the Shaolin monks exercises to strengthen their meditation — the seed of Shaolin kung fu — belongs to the ‌later layers, but it fixed his place in the martial imagination: the first patriarch as the first master of body-discipline. The *Yi Jin Jing* muscle-classic attaches itself to his name.

### The Round ​Wish-Keeper (Daruma Doll)

Japan made him a doll: round as the wall-sitter’s robe, weighted to right itself — *nanakorobi yaoki*, fall seven times, rise eight. You paint one blank eye when you make ‌a wish, the other when it comes true. The fierce Indian master ended as Japan’s most cheerful household god of perseverance, keeping his scowl and his self-righting bottom.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography ​associated with Bodhidharma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Wall-Gazing** — Nine years facing the wall at Shaolin; the tradition’s image of unmoving ‌resolve — and of the mind’s own wall.
- **The First Patriarch** — The twenty-eighth Indian patriarch who became China’s first — the wordless transmission passed through him.
- **Daruma’s Eyes** — The legend: he ​cut off his eyelids in wrath at sleep — and where they fell, tea plants grew. Japan’s doll watches with one eye.
- **The Bone of the Buddha** — His only transmission: a bowl, ​a robe, and a bone — the mind-to-mind seal outside the scriptures.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Bodhidharma survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus ‌is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

His supposed grave at Kongxiangsi in the Pagoda Forest of Shaolin carries the earliest memorials; the Shaolin steles ‌of the Tang dynasty name him. The Daruma doll’s manufacture is a modern industry, but the blank-eyed scowl descends from the Muromachi portraits.

## Realm & Domain

**Bodhidharma** is the First Patriarch of Zen: ‌the Indian prince-turned-monk who crossed the Pamirs to China around 520 CE, sat facing a wall at Shaolin for nine years, and transmitted the Buddha’s wordless teaching outside the scriptures. His legend is ​the bridge between India and East Asia — and the seed of martial, meditative, and cultural traditions that span the continent.

### The Wall-Gazing

Nine years facing the wall at Shaolin; the tradition’s image ​of unmoving resolve — and of the mind’s own wall.

### The First Patriarch

The twenty-eighth Indian patriarch who became China’s first — the wordless transmission passed through him.

### Daruma’s Eyes

The legend: he ‌cut off his eyelids in wrath at sleep — and where they fell, tea plants grew. Japan’s doll watches with one eye.

### The Bone of the Buddha

His only transmission: a bowl, a ​robe, and a bone — the mind-to-mind seal outside the scriptures.

## Across Cultures

Bodhidharma is the Silk Road made flesh: Indian dharma, Chinese wall, Japanese doll. The Zen lineages count him as the ​twenty-eighth Indian and first Chinese patriarch — the hinge of the transmission; and the Tibetan traditions remember him (as Bodhidharmottara) among the great siddhas. His defiance of the Liang emperor became the template ‌of the Zen master’s whole pedagogy.

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[caishen|Cáishén]], [[change|Chángé]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guandi|Guāndì]], and [[guanyin|Guānyīn]].

## Cultural Legacy

He stands at the head of every ​Zen lineage — Rinzai and Sōtō alike trace the wall; the Shaolin temple’s global fame rests on his legend; and the Daruma doll, with its self-righting scowl, is Japan’s most reproduced folk object. ​‘Zen’ as the West knows it begins, by the tradition’s own account, with his ‘don’t know’.

## A Meditation

Bodhidharma: the name is a doctrine — awakening-holding, the dharma that ‌holds itself awake. Restored plainly, it spans the journey it names: an Indian word, a Chinese wall, a Japanese doll, and the plain letters any reader can hold. Five syllables, one transmission.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Bodhidharma**, the map does not lead through diacritics or ​special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Chinese characters rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *bodhidharma* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is ​a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By ‌fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each ​character — **b**, **o**, **d**, **h**, **i**, **d**, **h**, **a**, **r**, **m**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" ​is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

**Bodhidharma** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is counted ​among 59 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Zen Patriarch, Wall-Gazer — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a ‌philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Bodhidharma**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a ​named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure ​and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Bodhidharma** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. ​When **Bodhidharma** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, ‌and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly ​in an article while the public web flattened it to *bodhidharma*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains ‌compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; ‌it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Bodhidharma**, the chain begins with the attested form in Chinese characters, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, ​and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Dharma of awakening" anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks would float free of the ​figure they name. The restored form **Bodhidharma** and the ASCII form *bodhidharma* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of lost diacritics or special ​characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Bodhidharma aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to ​every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is ‌the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
